originalTitle: Thetford residents remain on edge after days of ‘mob rule’ over asylum plans
summary: People voice frustration with officials’ failure to engage with community over placement of asylum seekers in area
content: A smashed window pane and some broken eggshells on a footpath were some of the tell-tale signs of events that took place this week on a residential street at the edge of Thetford. On Friday afternoon it was not hard to find local people with a sense of foreboding after the latest disorder in the Norfolk market town which has seen crowds attempt to break into properties believed to be housing asylum seekers. “The main concern is safety, the proximity of children and that people just have not been consulted about this,” said Jenny Hollis, a former councillor, who indicated the proximity of a local school and nursery to a – now seemingly vacant – house on the targeted street in the north of the town. “Thetford is a small town where people know each other, but if you are putting young men who people know nothing about into an area, sometimes in the dark of night, then it will be a cause of concern,” she said in reference to asylum seekers. For three nights, Thetford was the scene of protests and disorder, with police officers being subjected to violence, windows smashed, fences broken and people attempting to break into a residential property, police said. However, after unrest which the local MP said had “put Thetford back decades”, there was also deep unease among residents and others about the prospect of racism poisoning local relations, fuelled by disinformation and the role of the far right in seeking to exploit tensions. “I have lived here for more than a decade and have come to call it home,” said a woman, originally from eastern Europe, around the corner from where the latest unrest took place. “The people are lovely, but last week was the first time that my partner was shouted at by someone who derided him as a ‘migrant’.” Amid chants of “We want them out” from a crowd of up to 200 people on the targeted street on Wednesday night, a male police officer was hit by a brick and a female colleague was seriously bitten, Norfolk constabulary said. The number of arrests in connection with disorder in different parts of the town had risen to six as of Friday. Asylum seekers had been removed from properties on Thursday for their safety, according to the police, and there was no answer at a number of homes believed to have been used for that purpose when the Guardian visited. “I have HMOs [houses of multiple occupancy] with asylum seekers in them on both sides of my house,” said one man. They had tended to keep to themselves, he said, but he had concerns about tensions in the area and what it would do to property prices. The three nights of disorder threaten to become the spark for the type of anti-immigration tensions that boiled over last year around a hotel outside the Essex town of Epping and spread elsewhere. If the unrest in Thetford is different, however, it is that it marks the first time HMOs in England have become the target of concerted and organised anger. Terry Jermy, the MP for South West Norfolk and a rare Labour presence in what has traditionally been a Conservative-leaning region, has criticised what he described as a lack of engagement by the Home Office, and given voice to people’s unease that cheaper, working-class areas have been chosen as the location for housing asylum seekers in HMOs. “The lack of engagement both with the community and elected officials has been a huge concern, along with the apparent lack of a strategy, in terms of a cohesive plan, but also to close down rumours and the spread of misinformation,” said Jermy. “I have been happy to acknowledge people’s concerns and support peaceful protest but what we have seen over the last few days is outright criminality, mob rule and vigilante-style antics which go way beyond the rule of law. These people – and in many cases I’m talking about those who have travelled to Thetford – claim to be proud to be British, but to be proud to be British is to support the rule of law.” Criticism has persisted over the use of HMOs and the choice of locations to house asylum seekers, with protesters in Thetford targeting a list of houses believed to be used by Serco, a company that has a multimillion pound contract with the Home Office. Social media accounts operated by prominent far-right activists, including Stephen Yaxley-Lennon – who calls himself Tommy Robinson – have disseminated footage from the protests. In one clip, a man can be seen directing crowds to an address where he said there were “invaders”, a term used by Robinson and others. In answer to the allegation it had mishandled its contract, a spokesperson for Serco said it worked under the direction of the Home Office, which tells it the number of people it expects to house in local authority areas based on overall national levels of demand. The Home Office has insisted the use of “large sites” is a key part of its strategy, and said the population of asylum seekers in hotels fell by 35% in the past year and by 63% from the peak of 56,000 in 2023. Figures from Reform UK have taken a prominent interest in the opposition to the use of HMOs. Scott Hussey, a member of the cabinet on Reform-controlled Norfolk county council, was at the scene on Friday, and said residents were frustrated at seeing their town being turned into “a dumping ground for illegal immigrants”. He said his understanding from meeting with the Home Office was that more HMOs were going to be sited in Thetford,and that this would add to tensions over proposals to use a nearby RAF base to house asylum seekers. Those who protested in Thetford this week included participants in a regular protest outside RAF Barnham, outside the town. Plans to house 3,750 migrants at the former base were revealed in June. chineseTitle: 经过数天对庇护计划的“暴民统治”后，塞特福德居民仍处于紧张状态
chineseSummary: 人们对官员未能就寻求庇护者在该地区的安置问题与社区进行接触表示失望
chineseContent: 本周在塞特福德边缘的一条住宅街道上发生的事件中，一块被打碎的窗玻璃和人行道上的一些破碎的蛋壳是一些明显的迹象。周五下午，在诺福克集镇最近发生骚乱后，不难发现当地人有一种不祥的预感，人群试图闯入据信为寻求庇护者提供住房的房屋。前议员珍妮·霍利斯 (Jenny Hollis) 表示：“主要的担忧是安全、儿童的接近性以及人们在这方面没有得到咨询。”她表示，当地一所学校和托儿所距离该镇北部目标街道上的一所房屋（现已看似空置）很近。 “塞特福德是一个小镇，人们互相认识，但如果你把人们一无所知的年轻人放入一个地区，有时是在漆黑的夜晚，那么这将引起人们的担忧，”她在谈到寻求庇护者时说。警方表示，塞特福德连续三个晚上都发生了抗议和骚乱，警察遭受暴力，窗户被砸碎，栅栏被破坏，人们试图闯入住宅区。然而，当地议员称骚乱“让塞特福德倒退了几十年”之后，居民和其他人也对种族主义毒害当地关系的前景深感不安，而虚假信息和极右翼势力试图利用紧张局势，加剧了种族主义的前景。 “我在这里住了十多年，已经把这里称为家了，”一位来自东欧的女士说道，她就在最近的骚乱发生地附近。 “这里的人很可爱，但上周我的伴侣第一次被人大喊大叫，嘲笑他是‘移民’。”在一群人高呼“我们希望他们离开”的声音中
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于全球新闻信号，适合用于观察外部环境、政策变化、地缘风险和市场情绪。
